files.about:
The command palette: quick access to everything an app can do, from the keyboard. A dialog near the top of the
window with one field and the list of commands under it; typing narrows the list, the arrows move, Enter runs the
command and closes the palette, Esc closes it. Each command shows its own key at the end of its row, as plain text
(R5), so the palette also teaches the keys. After Imago's `openPalette`, which every app of the suite opens with
Ctrl+K from a button of its title bar.
The commands are the app's: the palette knows none. Given no list, it shows the commands the app declared in its
registry (`CommandsProvider`, `useCommand`), by group, those that cannot be done now dimmed, and the registry opens it
with Ctrl+K. A command is found by its name and by its `keywords`; every word typed has to be in one of the two. The highlighted row is the one language of every list (`ROW_HIGHLIGHT`).
A command that chooses one of several (`checked`: light, dark, the system's look) is an option checked or not: the one
in use has a check at the end of its row, in the ink (R2), the look of `Combobox`'s chosen option; for a screen reader
it is `aria-checked` on the option, because `aria-selected` marks the highlighted row. The others keep the check's
room, so a key after it does not move.

props.name: commands
props.doc: What it lists. Absent: the commands declared in the registry (`useCommand`), by group, those that cannot be done now dimmed.

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the palette and the placeholder of its field. Absent: the toolkit's words («Type a command»).

props.name: emptyText
props.doc: Said when no command holds the text. Absent: the toolkit's words.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The palette fades in (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

fields.name: label
fields.doc: What it does, as the user would say it («Go to Settings»).

fields.name: shortcut
fields.doc: Its own key («Ctrl F»), shown at the end of the row. The app binds it.

fields.name: group
fields.doc: The heading it sits under («Go to», «Look»). Commands of one group follow each other.

fields.name: icon
fields.doc: A 16px drawing before the name.

fields.name: keywords
fields.doc: Other words it is found by.

fields.name: checked
fields.doc: For a command that chooses one of several: true for the one in use (a check at the end of its row, `aria-checked`), false for the others. Absent: not a choice.

types.name: CommandPaletteOpenness
types.doc: Open and closed by the app, or both absent: then the registry's own state (`CommandsProvider`), which Ctrl+K opens.

files.about:
The commands of an app in one registry: an app declares each command once, near the state it acts on (`useCommand`),
with its name, its group, its key and whether it can be done now; the key runs it from anywhere in the window, the
palette lists it (`CommandPalette` with no list), and Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac) opens the palette in every app. After
Imago's command registry (`createRegistry`, `mountApp`), which every app of the suite declares its commands in.
- A key is written as `KeyboardEvent.key` names it, after `Ctrl`, `Alt` and `Shift`: «Escape», «F6», «Ctrl+F»,
  «Ctrl+Shift+T», «Shift+?», «Ctrl++». `Ctrl` is Cmd on a Mac (Control stays the system's there), and the key is shown
  in the words of the system and the app's language («Ctrl F», «Cmd F», «Strg F»). A letter or a digit is also found
  by its place on the keyboard when the layout writes another sign there (Cyrillic, Option on a Mac); a digit or a
  sign is found whatever Shift it took (AZERTY), and a sign typed with AltGr is not read as Ctrl+Alt.
- Where a key belongs to what has the focus, it is left there: in a field, a plain key (but Escape and the function
  keys) and Ctrl or Alt with a key that moves the caret; on a control, Enter, Space and the keys that move inside it;
  in an open surface (a dialog, a menu, a list of options), a key with neither Ctrl nor Alt; a plain key a widget
  already handled (`preventDefault`, or not let through with `stopPropagation`); and every key in the places
  `ownKeysIn` names (a terminal, a code editor). A combination another handler refused (`useDesktopGuard` refuses
  the browser's Ctrl+F) still runs the app's command: the browser's use of the key is what was refused.
- A command whose `when` is false does not run, and the palette shows it dimmed, so the list does not jump.
- A command that chooses one of several (light, dark or the system's look: `useSchemeCommands`) says whether it is the
  one in use (`checked`): the palette marks it with a check in the ink, as a chosen option of a list.
- The registry is in the order the commands are declared in the tree; when two available commands share a key, the
  one declared last runs.
- `KeyHints`, in the window's foot, names the keys that work now of the commands the app picks (R5: plain text,
  hidden on a phone).
- An app that is one part of a larger page (a sample in a gallery, a widget) names its own place (`keysIn`): its keys
  run only while the focus is inside it, so two apps on one page do not both answer one key.

components.name: CommandsProvider
components.doc: The registry of an app's commands, around the whole app (outside `AppShell`): it runs their keys, holds the palette's open state for a `CommandPalette` with no list, and holds Ctrl+K itself.

props.name: ownKeysIn
props.doc: A selector for the places that keep their own keys (`'.xterm, .cm-editor'`): there no command's key runs.

props.name: palette
props.doc: Whether Ctrl+K opens the registry's palette (default true). False leaves Ctrl+K to an app that opens its palette itself.

props.name: keysIn

components.name: KeyHints
components.doc: The keys that work now, for the window's foot (`AppShell`'s `footer`): each named command that has a key and can be done now, its key as plain text and its name («Ctrl K Commands»). A command that cannot be done now leaves the list and comes back with it. Hidden on a phone, where there is no keyboard to press them on. In a narrow foot the hints that do not fit are left out whole, from the last: none is cut in the middle of a word.

props.name: ids
props.doc: What it names, in this order: a command by its id (shown when it has a key and can be done now; `PALETTE_COMMAND` names Ctrl+K), or a key that is not a command (`{ keys: 'F6', label: 'Next region' }`).

files.about:
The thread of a conversation with an assistant (or with a person): the column that scrolls. It stays at the last
message while the reader is there, so an answer being written is followed, and it stops following as soon as the
reader moves up, by however little; a button then leads back to the latest message. What is in it are the turns
(`Message`), and what an assistant did on the way (`Reasoning`, `ToolCall`); the field under it is `PromptInput`.
Screen readers meet the thread as a log: while an answer is being written (`busy`) the log waits, so the answer is
read once, whole, and not word by word.
Nothing moves by itself: no typing dots, no shimmer. That an answer is on its way is said by the stop button of
`PromptInput` and by the row of `Reasoning`. Following the answer and going back to its end are done at once, never
as a glide: a long way across the screen is not a movement of this toolkit. The button back, which the reader's own
scroll brings up, enters as a hint does when motion is on.

components.name: Conversation

that are images. A window that takes most of the screen, the picture whole in it (never cropped), its caption under

their places and are off at the two ends (R14). The left and right arrows do the same; Esc and the close button
close it. The app holds which picture is on (`index`) and whether the window is open.
A file with pages, zoom and «open the original» is an `AttachmentViewer`; this is for pictures that are just looked at.

The look settings of an app (owner, 2026-11-20): one base colour makes the palette, three combinations share it out,
three tones set how lively it is. Every choice is a card with a preview of what it does; the app passes its own words.
The icons are not a choice: Sigrid has one set, the same in every app (2026-11-23). The ready-made themes are the finer choice, for the app's «Advanced» fold.
The density (compact, normal, large, or an app's own) is a choice of the same family: each card draws three rows to scale.

then scrolls; under it a row with the app's own tools at the start (attach a file, choose a model) and, at the end,
the one button that sends. While an answer is being written (`busy`) that same button, in the same place, stops it:
the control never moves (R14). Enter sends and Shift+Enter makes a new line; with a finger Enter makes a new line,
as a phone's keyboard does, and the button sends. An empty message is not sent.
Form: one field (`lib/field.ts`): the border of a field around the text and its row, and the focus ring on that
border while the text has the focus. The send button is the solid action: on a chat screen it is the one primary
(R3); the stop button is `outline`.

Light, dark and the system's look as three commands of the registry, the same in every app of the suite (owner,
2026-11-23): the person chooses the scheme from the palette, and no app writes commands or theme code for it. The app
calls `useSchemeCommands` inside its `CommandsProvider` with its look (its theme, and the user's tone or own colours
when it has them) and the key of the browser's storage the choice is kept under. The three commands sit in a group of
their own («Look», `useWords().scheme`), each with its icon (R6) and a name that stands alone without the heading
(«Light theme»: a screen reader says the row, not the group); the one in use is checked. Choosing one puts the theme
in that scheme on the document's root at once (`applyTheme`) and keeps it. The pages and the tabs that keep the choice
under the same key follow it, and the system's choice, the default, follows `prefers-color-scheme` while the page is
open. A value kept that is not light, dark or the system's is the system's. The storage is the answer whenever it can
be read; only where the browser gives no storage at all does a choice hold in the page, until it is closed.
`applyKeptScheme`, called in the app's entry before React renders, puts the kept choice on the root as soon as that
script runs. On a server nothing reads the browser's storage: the choice is the system's, drawn light. After Imago's
`mountApp`, whose palette had the same commands.

types.name: SchemeState
types.doc: The choice, and the scheme drawn now (for the system's choice, the one the system says).

A deck of cards decided one at a time, each to one of two sides: keep or skip, approve or refuse, now or later.
One card, one decision: nothing else on the screen asks for attention while a pile is sorted.
Three ways to decide, all the same decision: drag the card past a third of the way (or flick it) and let go; press
the left or right arrow with the card in focus; or press one of the two buttons under the deck, which are always
there and never move (R14), so nothing depends on a gesture. While the card is dragged far enough, the word of the
side it would go to shows on it: what letting go will do is said before it is done.
The deck keeps nothing: the app holds the cards (`items`, the first is on top) and takes the decided one out when
`onSwipe` tells it; to take a decision back it puts the card first again (an `Undo` in a notice, `Toasts`). A card
the app leaves in comes back to its place.
The app takes the card out as `onSwipe` runs, and puts it back if saving the decision fails: a card taken out
later is seen once more at rest before it goes.
The card follows the finger at once (that is the gesture, not an animation); thrown, it leaves with a movement, and
let go before the mark it comes back with one, only when motion is on (`animated`, or `MotionProvider`). The next
card lies under the top one, still: the flat page has no stack that zooms.

components.name: SwipeDeck
components.doc: A deck of cards decided one at a time, to the left or to the right.

props.name: items
props.doc: The cards still to decide; the first is on top. The app takes a card out when it is decided.

props.name: getKey
props.doc: What tells a card from the others.

props.name: getLabel
props.doc: The card's name for screen readers (its title).

props.name: children
props.doc: What a card shows: laid out with the toolkit's parts (`Heading`, `Text`, `DescriptionList`).

props.name: onSwipe
props.doc: A card was decided: the app takes it out of `items` as this runs (and offers Undo in a notice), and puts it back if the decision could not be saved.

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the deck for screen readers («Requests to review»).

props.name: leftLabel
props.doc: What each side means, in a word or two («Skip», «Keep»): the buttons under the deck, and the word on a dragged card.

props.name: leftIcon
props.doc: The icons of the two buttons. Default the two arrows.

props.name: empty
props.doc: What takes the deck's place when no card is left (an `Empty`). Absent: the toolkit's words.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: No card can be decided (while a decision is being saved).

props.name: animated
props.doc: The thrown card leaves with a movement, and a card let go early comes back with one. Absent: as `MotionProvider` says.

The theme gallery: a compact picker of the app's themes, one tile each. A tile is drawn in its own theme, in the
scheme and tone the app shows now (`themeVariables` on the tile alone): its name on the theme's primary fill, then a
small sketch of a window (the sidebar with a chosen row, two rows, a button), so the person sees the theme before
choosing it. The tiles are one radio group: one Tab stop, the arrows, Home and End move and choose (`radioArrows`, as
the look settings' cards), and the chosen tile has the accent edge and a check in a dot (the choice is not shown by
the edge alone). An optional last tile, dashed, stands for a theme of the person's own: choosing it calls the app,
which opens its own editor; it is the chosen one when `selected` is null. Two columns, three from 352px of its own
width (a container query: it fits a narrow settings panel).

components.name: ThemeGallery
components.doc: A compact theme picker. Each tile samples its own surfaces in the active scheme and tone. A null selection marks the optional custom tile, whose editor belongs to the caller.

Park UI (MIT) tree-view 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/tree-view.ts)
A tree of rows: things that hold other things (folders and files, sections and pages, any hierarchy), each a row with
its name, one of Sigrid's icons, a short fact and a count at its end, and the rows it holds under it, one level in.
Behaviour: Ark UI's TreeView. The rows are one Tab stop (the chosen row when it is in sight); Down and Up move, Right
opens a branch and then goes into it, Left closes it and then goes out to the branch that holds the row, Home and End
reach the first and the last row in sight, the first letters of a name reach it, `*` opens the branches beside the
row; Enter, Space or a press choose a row, and on a branch also open or close it (with `onOpen`, Enter asks the app and
does not fold: Right and Left do). One row is chosen, never several. In a language written from the right, Right and
Left swap. Enter, Space, Right and Left with Shift, Ctrl, Alt or Meta held are not the tree's.
The row that has the focus is the `treeitem` itself, with its level, whether it is open and whether it is chosen: on a
branch Ark's control is made the `treeitem`, and the rows it holds are its `group` (`aria-owns`). A closed branch's
rows are not in the page.
Branches whose children the app loads (`hasChildren` and `loadChildren`) load them when they are opened: the row says
«Loading» meanwhile and takes no second opening (Enter and Right do nothing on it), and if the load fails it says so
and stays closed, so opening it again tries again. The tree loads them itself, not through Ark, which would keep a
branch «loaded» for ever: children belong to the node object they were loaded for, and when the app gives another
object for that id (another project, the same folder read again), or none, they are dropped.
The filter (`query`, typed in the field of `search` or given by the app) keeps what `match` finds (by default: the name
holds the text) with all it holds, and the branches that lead to a find, opened. What the person opens or closes
meanwhile is theirs: when the filter is cleared their own branches come back, with those changes.
Form: Park's `tree-view` recipe on the toolkit's tokens: rows of the density's row height (44px with a finger), l2,
14px, one level in 20px (Park's 22px, on the 4px grid). At the start the chevron of the sidebar's groups (14px in a
16px slot, a quarter turn when open, turning only with `animated`), then the icon, the name, and at the end the fact
in 12px tabular figures and a `Count` (R5). The row's look is that of every list of things (`lib/rows.ts`, as
`ItemRow`): under the pointer a share of the selection tint; the chosen row has the whole tint, its ink and the short
accent bar at its start (R1), and its name in semibold. Not taken from Park: the chevron in the accent (R2: it is
chrome, in the muted ink), the semibold of the first level (semibold says «chosen»), the line that guides the eye
down a branch, the transitions.
What a row draws is memoised: a move of the focus paints Ark's own parts again (its context is new at each move), not
the icons, names and facts of every row.
A row may be `disabled`: it stays in sight and in the keys' way, says so (`aria-disabled`), is drawn quieter, and is
neither chosen, opened, closed nor taken by `onOpen`.
`onOpen` is the app's own «do the thing»: Enter, or a double press, on a row, besides the choice (a file opens in an
editor, a folder is entered); it does not open or close a branch (Right and Left do, and a single press). `followFocus`
makes the choice follow the focus as the arrows move it, for a tree that is the list of a list and its details.
`onKeyDown` is asked first about a key on a row, for the app's own keys (`j` and `k` that move the choice): when it calls
`preventDefault()` the tree does nothing with the key. `typeahead={false}` leaves the letters to the app. When the app
changes `selected` (a key of its own), the tree scrolls to the row (with `virtual`) and, if the focus is in the tree, takes
it there, so the keys that follow are on the row chosen.
`virtual` draws only the rows in sight, for thousands of rows: the open branches are laid flat (each row says its
level, its place among its siblings and the size of the group: the tree of a screen reader is the same), the room of
the rows not drawn is kept as padding, and a row the keys reach is scrolled to and takes the focus when it is drawn. The
row with the focus stays in the page when it is scrolled out of sight, while the focus is in the tree, so the keys do not
fall to the page after a turn of the wheel.
The rows are all as tall as the first one, which is read where it is drawn. The box needs a height: `fill` takes the one of the region that holds it
(a pane, a `Panel`'s body), so an app writes no class for it. This is its own small windowing, not TanStack Virtual (`VirtualList`, `./virtual`): this entry must stay free of libraries.
It is not the graph: `GraphCanvas` and its tree mode draw things joined by lines; this is a list of nested rows, and
the two share no code.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: Name of the tree for screen readers («Files»).

props.name: nodes
props.doc: The first level of the tree. Children loaded for a node stay while the app gives the same node object: build the nodes once (a constant, state, `useMemo`), and give a new object for a node whose children must be read again (another project, a refresh).

props.name: selected
props.doc: The chosen row, by its id, or null for none. With it the choice is the app's: pass the id `onSelect` gives.

props.name: defaultSelected
props.doc: The row chosen at first, when the choice is the tree's own.

props.name: onSelect
props.doc: The person chose a row (a press, Enter or Space): its id, and the node.

props.name: onOpen
props.doc: The person asks to open the thing (Enter, or a double press, on a row): its id, and the node. Besides the choice, which it does not replace; it does not open or close a branch (Right, Left and a single press do). Not for a `disabled` row.

props.name: followFocus
props.doc: The choice follows the focus: moving it with the arrows chooses the row it reaches, as in a list that shows details beside it. Absent: the choice is made by a press, Enter or Space. `onSelect` is heard once for each move.

props.name: onKeyDown
props.doc: A key on a row, before the tree takes it: the app's own keys (`j` and `k` to move the choice, Delete). `event.preventDefault()` makes the tree do nothing with the key. The id is the row's.

props.name: typeahead
props.doc: The first letters typed reach a row by its name. Default on; `false` leaves the letters to the app (`onKeyDown`).

props.name: virtual
props.doc: Only the rows in sight are in the page: for thousands of rows. The box needs a height: `fill`, or `className`.

props.name: fill
props.doc: As tall as the region that holds it, which gives it its height (the content of the frame, a pane, a `Panel`'s body, a `Column fill`): the rows scroll inside it, and a field of the filter keeps its place above them. The height `virtual` needs.

props.name: expanded
props.doc: The branches the person opened, by id. With it they are the app's: pass the list `onExpandedChange` gives. The branches the filter opens are not in it. A branch still to load stays closed until the person opens it.

props.name: defaultExpanded
props.doc: The branches open at first, when they are the tree's own.

props.name: onExpandedChange
props.doc: The person opened or closed a branch: the whole list of the branches they opened. A branch that loads joins it once its rows are here. Not called when the list did not change.

props.name: loadChildren
props.doc: Loads the rows of a branch with `hasChildren`, when it is first opened. A promise that fails leaves the branch closed, saying so; opening it again tries again. The signal says the tree no longer waits (the node changed or left, the tree left the page).

props.name: search
props.doc: A field above the rows that filters them (`query`).

props.name: searchLabel
props.doc: The name and placeholder of that field. Absent: the toolkit's words («Filter by name»).

props.name: query
props.doc: The text that filters the rows. With it the text is the app's: pass what `onQueryChange` gives. It filters with the tree's field (`search`) or without it, from a field of the app's (`ToolbarSearch`). Only spaces, or nothing: no filter.

props.name: defaultQuery
props.doc: The text the filter starts with, when it is the tree's own.

props.name: onQueryChange
props.doc: The text of the filter changed: typed in the tree's field, or cleared.

props.name: match
props.doc: Whether a node is found by the text, given as it is (`query`), only when it holds more than spaces. Absent: its name holds the text, whatever the case and the spaces at its ends. A node found shows with all it holds; a branch that leads to one shows with what it keeps, opened. Branches never loaded are not searched: to have them searched, give their children. An app counts the finds with the same function over its own nodes. A constant, or memoised: a new function filters again.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The chevron of a branch turns when it opens or closes, as the sidebar's groups (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

types.name: TreeNode
types.doc: A thing of the tree: a row, and the rows it holds.

fields.name: id
fields.doc: Names the thing among all the others of the tree (a path, a key): the choice and the open branches are ids.

fields.name: name
fields.doc: What the row says; the filter by default and the first letters typed look for it.

fields.name: icon
fields.doc: A meaning of Sigrid's icons (`folder`, `file`…); a name Sigrid does not draw is an empty slot. In a tree where some rows have one, a row without keeps an empty slot (R6).

fields.name: openIcon
fields.doc: The icon of a branch while it is open (`folderOpen` for a `folder`). Absent: `icon`, open or closed.

fields.name: image
fields.doc: A picture of the thing, where it has one of its own (the logo of a service, of a framework): the address of an SVG or a PNG the app serves, drawn in the icon's slot with `Logo`, 16px and whole. The row's icon is in its place while it loads and when it fails. The name of the row says what it is: the picture says nothing to screen readers.

fields.name: meta
fields.doc: A short fact at the end of the row, in tabular figures: a size, a date.

fields.name: count
fields.doc: How many things the node holds or waits on (changed, unread): a `Count` at the end of the row, after `meta`. Zero shows nothing.

fields.name: children
fields.doc: The rows it holds. With an array (even empty) the row is a branch, which opens and closes.

fields.name: hasChildren
fields.doc: It holds rows the app loads when the branch is opened (`loadChildren`), until then unknown. Read only without `children`; without `loadChildren` the branch holds nothing.

fields.name: disabled
fields.doc: The row is there but cannot be chosen, opened or closed, nor taken by `onOpen`: drawn quieter, and still reached by the keys.

A path of steps taken one at a time: a form too long for one screen, a setup, a signup. One question on the
screen, the path above it (`Steps`: where one is, what is done, what is left), and two buttons at its foot that
never move (R14): «Back» at the start, off on the first step, and the one solid button at the end, «Continue»
until the last step and then the app's own word («Create the account»).
The app holds where the person is (`current`) and what they answered; the wizard draws the step and asks to move.
A step that is not answered yet keeps the person there: its button is off (`canContinue: false`), and the app says
what is missing in the step itself. A step already done is a button of the path: going back never loses an answer,
since the answers are the app's. Enter in a field of the step goes on, as in any form.
When the step changes, its title takes the focus, so a screen reader reads where it now is; with motion on the
step comes in from the side it was asked from.

components.name: Wizard
components.doc: A path of steps taken one at a time, with the path above the step and two buttons at its foot.

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the path for screen readers («Signup»).

props.name: current
props.doc: The step on the screen, counting from 0, which the app holds.

props.name: onFinish
props.doc: The last step was confirmed.

props.name: finishLabel
props.doc: The word of the button of the last step («Create the account»). Absent: the toolkit's word («Finish»).

props.name: busy
props.doc: The last step is being saved: its button waits in its place.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The step comes in with a movement, and the buttons answer the press. Absent: as `MotionProvider` says.

props.name: children
props.doc: What the step on the screen asks: its fields, drawn by the app for that step.

types.name: WizardStep
types.doc: One step of a path.

fields.name: label
fields.doc: The name of the step in the path («Account», «Plan»): short.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: The question of the step, as its title when it is the one on the screen. Absent: its `label`.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: A line under the title: what is asked, and why.

fields.name: canContinue
fields.doc: `false` while the step is not answered: the button that goes on is off. Default `true`.

files.about:
The tree of a workspace and what is done to it (`Workspace` draws it): panes in a split tree, each leaf a group of
tabs. Plain data, so an app keeps it, saves it as JSON and restores it; every function here is pure and gives back a
new tree, or the very same one when there is nothing to change, so an app can tell by `===` whether to save.
- A `split` puts its children side by side (`horizontal`: the first at the start of the line) or one under the other
  (`vertical`), each as wide or as tall as its `weight` is of all of them. Weights are ratios, not pixels.
- A `tabs` is a group: its tabs in order and the one chosen (`activeId`, null with no tabs). The ids of the groups and
  of the tabs are the app's, and each is unique in the tree.
- The tree is always normal (`normalizeWorkspace`): no group is empty unless it is the only one, no split has a single
  child or a child that splits the same way (it is folded in), every weight is a positive number, every group names a
  tab that is in it. Each function that changes the tree gives it back normal.
- Where a tab goes is a `WorkspaceDrop`: into a group at a slot, or to an edge of a group, which divides that group
  and puts the tab in a new one beside it. The same value is what a drop of the pointer and a key of the keyboard say.
- Geometry is in fractions of the whole workspace (`layoutWorkspace`): the groups' boxes, the sashes between them and
  the nearest group in a direction, so the drawing, the drop targets and the keyboard read one source.

types.name: WorkspaceDrop
types.doc: Where a tab is put. In a group, at a slot of its strip (`index`: before the tab now at that place, the end when absent). Or at an edge of a group: the group is divided there and the tab goes into a new group, named `newId`.

types.name: WorkspaceLayout
types.doc: What the geometry of a tree says: the box of each group (by id) and the sashes.

types.name: WorkspaceNode
types.doc: A pane (a group of tabs) or a division of panes.

types.name: WorkspaceRect
types.doc: A box in fractions (0 to 1) of the workspace: `x` and `y` from its start and top.

types.name: WorkspaceSash
types.doc: A line between two children of a split, in the same fractions.

fields.name: path
fields.doc: The split it divides.

fields.name: boundary
fields.doc: Between the children `boundary` and `boundary + 1`.

fields.name: at
fields.doc: Where the line is: `x` for a `horizontal` split (a vertical line), `y` for a `vertical` one.

fields.name: from
fields.doc: Where it starts and how long it is across the split.

fields.name: span
fields.doc: How much of the workspace the split takes along its direction: what a distance moved is a fraction of.

fields.name: weights
fields.doc: The split's weights now.

types.name: WorkspaceSplit
types.doc: A division: `children` in a line, each with its `weights` share. There are at least two children and as many weights.

types.name: WorkspaceTab
types.doc: A tab: what its title says, an icon if it has one, and whether it can be closed (default yes). An app may add its own fields (`WorkspaceTab` is what the parts need).

types.name: WorkspaceTabs
types.doc: A group of tabs: a pane. `activeId` is the tab shown, `null` when the group has none.

files.about:
A tiling area: panes in a split tree, each pane a group of tabs, the person making the layout (a terminal beside the
code, the code over a log). The app owns the tree, plain data (`WorkspaceNode`, `workspace-model.ts`), and is told of
every change (`onChange`); the area draws it and what is in each tab is the app's (`renderTab`).
- Nothing in a tab is lost by moving things: the content of every tab is drawn once, in one flat list keyed by the
  tab, and placed over the box of its pane; so a tab dragged to another pane, a pane divided or closed around it, keeps
  its content mounted (a terminal keeps running, a page keeps its state). The tabs that are not shown stay mounted,
  hidden (`keepMounted="active"` unmounts them). The panes are laid out by percent, from the weights, with no
  measuring; only a drag of a divider measures.
- A divider is a window splitter like `SplitPane`'s: one tab stop, `role="separator"` with the share of its first
  neighbour (`aria-valuenow`), the pointer moves it and the pane follows, the arrows move it 16px (Shift, 64px), Home and
  End take it to the least each neighbour keeps (`minSize`), a double press shares the two alike. The arrows follow
  the panes in a language written from the right. The weights are told once, when the pointer is let go.
- A tab is chosen with a press or the arrows (the strip is `Tabs`, so one tab stop and Home/End), closed with its ×,
  Delete or a middle press (`onCloseTab` lets the app ask first), and put in order or in another pane by hand: a
  drag shows where it will go (a mark in a strip to put it in that place, the middle of a pane to join it, a side of a
  pane to divide it there, with a box that says so; Escape drops it). The same is done without a pointer: Shift+←/→ puts
  it earlier or later, Alt+Shift+arrow divides the pane in that direction (a pane's only tab joins the pane there),
  and the tab's menu (right button, Menu key) lists them with Close; a polite status says where it went. A strip that
  is longer than the pane scrolls and brings the chosen tab into sight.
- A pane is the focused one while the person works in it (`focusedId`, told with `onFocusedChange`); with
  `onMaximizedChange` its bar has a button that fills the whole area with it, the others stay mounted.

props.name: tree
props.doc: The layout: panes and their tabs. The app keeps it and passes what `onChange` gives.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: The person changed the layout: a tab chosen, closed, moved or divided off, a divider moved. Not told for what the app itself did to the tree.

props.name: renderTab
props.doc: The content of a tab. It is called for every tab, shown or not (see `keepMounted`), so keep it light and let the content keep its own state.

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the area for screen readers («Terminals»).

props.name: keepMounted
props.doc: `all` (the default): every tab stays mounted, hidden when it is not shown. `active`: only the shown tab of each pane is drawn.

props.name: empty
props.doc: What a pane with no tab shows. Default: the toolkit's sentence, and a button when `onAddTab` is given.

props.name: onAddTab
props.doc: The bar of each pane has a button that adds a tab; this is told which pane. The app makes the tab and puts it in the tree (`addWorkspaceTab`).

props.name: onCloseTab
props.doc: A tab's close was asked (its ×, Delete, a middle press, the menu). Given, the app decides (it may ask first, and closes with `closeWorkspaceTab`); absent, the tab closes.

props.name: tabMenu
props.doc: The app's own entries of a tab's menu, above the toolkit's.

props.name: focusedId
props.doc: The pane the person works in, when the app keeps it; otherwise the area keeps it (the first at first).

props.name: onFocusedChange
props.doc: The person began to work in another pane (a press or the focus went in).

props.name: maximizedId
props.doc: The pane that fills the whole area, `null` for none, when the app keeps it. With `onMaximizedChange` each bar has the button.

props.name: minSize
props.type: { width?: number | undefined; height?: number | undefined; }
props.doc: The least width and height of a pane, in px, a divider keeps. Default 160 by 120.

props.name: newGroupId
props.doc: Makes the id of a pane the person divides off. Default: `pane-1`, `pane-2`… the first that the tree does not have.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The chosen tab's tint slides to a new tab, and the card of a menu and a hint fades in (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

types.name: WorkspaceTabState
types.doc: What a tab's content is told about its place.

fields.name: active
fields.doc: The tab is the one its pane shows.

fields.name: visible
fields.doc: It is on screen: shown by its pane, and its pane is not hidden behind a maximized one. A terminal fits itself when this turns true.

fields.name: focused
fields.doc: Its pane is the one the person works in.

files.about:
A table of data, ready to use: columns that sort when their heading is pressed, one row that can be chosen, and,
for thousands of rows, only the ones in sight in the page. The behaviour is TanStack's (`@tanstack/react-table` for
the columns and the sorting, `@tanstack/react-virtual` for the rows in sight: npm dependencies, pinned, see
THIRD_PARTY.md); the form is the toolkit's `Table` parts. It lives in its own entry of the package (`./table`), so
an app without a table does not load either library.
- A column says its heading, what a cell shows, and the value it sorts by. Without that value the heading is a
  word and not a button. A press sorts up, a second down, a third puts the rows back as they were given. The
  heading says how it is sorted with `aria-sort`, and with an arrow for the eye.
- With `onRowPress` a row is pressed with the pointer or with Enter and Space; the arrows, Home and End move among
  the rows, which are one Tab stop, as in a list: the row that had the focus last, or the chosen one, or the first
  in sight (the check and the caret of a row are not Tab stops of their own, and give the focus back to the row
  when pressed). A press on a control inside a cell (a button, a link, a field) is that control's and not the row's.
  The chosen row (`current`) has the selection tint (R1).
- With `virtual` the box needs a height (`className="h-96"`): the rows outside it are not in the page, two spacer
  rows keep the scrollbar honest, and each row is measured as it is drawn, so any density and a finger's 44px hold.
  Home and End go to the first and the last row of the data. A row scrolled far out of sight is no longer in the
  page, except the one that has the focus, which stays while the focus is in the table (so the keys do not fall to
  the page after a turn of the wheel); once the focus leaves, Tab comes back to a row in sight. The box keeps clear of
  the headings that stay in sight (and of a group's) when it scrolls to a row, whether the browser or the library does.
- `columns` is best made once (outside the component, or with `useMemo`): a new array at every paint sorts the
  rows again at every paint.
- A tree and a choice (the list of things to clean up, a folder with what is in it): `rowLevel` gives a row its level
  (1 is the first) and indents its first cell by it, `rowOpen` says of a row that holds others whether it is open
  (`undefined`: it holds none) and puts a caret before its first cell, `onRowOpenChange` hears the caret and the keys
  (Right opens a closed row and, on an open one, goes to its first row; Left closes an open row and, on any other, goes
  to the row that holds it; they swap in a language written from the right); the app puts in `rows` only the rows in
  sight, the children of an open row, in the order it wants them.
  `isGroupRow` makes a row a group: one cell across every column, which stays in sight under the headings while its
  rows scroll (`groupCell` is what it says: a name, a count, a size), foldable like any row that holds others; with
  `virtual` the heading of the group in sight stays in the page even when its own row is far above. With any of them
  the table is a `treegrid`: each row says its level, its place among its siblings (`aria-posinset`, `aria-setsize`),
  whether it is open and, with `selection`, whether it is chosen (a row of which only some are chosen says nothing
  of it, and its check says «mixed»).
- A tree is ordered by the app, not by the table: with levels, folds or groups (or with `manualSort`) a press on a
  heading still says how the app is asked to sort (the button, `aria-sort`, `onSortChange`) but the rows are shown as
  given, so a child never leaves its parent.
- `selection` adds a column of checks, one for each row, and in the heading one for all: `isSelected` says `true`,
  `false` or `'mixed'` (a group of which some rows are chosen, shown as a dash), `onSelectedChange` hears the check, and
  `selectAll` and `onSelectAll` are the heading's (the check that chooses all goes there, never in the `header` of a
  column, where it would sit inside the sort button). It is the app that holds what is chosen.
- `onRowKeyDown` is asked first about a key on a row: an app key (Enter opens a folder) is taken there and
  `preventDefault()` keeps the table from taking it too; for every key the app leaves, the table does what it did
  (Enter presses the row, Space too, or ticks it when there is a `selection`; the arrows, Home, End, PageUp and PageDown
  move; none of them with Alt, Ctrl or Meta held). `containerRef` is the box that scrolls, for an app that reads its
  scrolling.
- A row may have no check (`isSelected` gives `null`: a sub-heading that cannot be chosen) or a check that cannot be
  pressed now (`isDisabled`, `selectAllDisabled`: a blocked row, a job that holds the list). `fill` makes the box as tall
  as the place that holds it, so that the table is the content of a panel and its headings stay in sight.
An app that needs more of a table (filters, pinned columns, groups) drives TanStack Table itself and draws it with
`Table`, `TableRow` and `TableCell`: this component is the common case, not a wall around the library.

files.about:
The thread of a long conversation, of which only the messages in sight are in the page: `Conversation` for ten
thousand turns, each of its own height (a line, or an answer of a screenful). It is `Conversation` in every other
way: a log with a name that waits while an answer is written, that stays at the latest message while the reader is
at the end (an answer being written is followed, and it opens at the end), that stops following as soon as the reader
moves up, and a button back to the latest message. The messages are given as a count and a function that draws the
one at a place, as `VirtualList` does, and each is measured as it is drawn and watched (`VirtualList variable`, on
TanStack Virtual: it has its own entry of the package, `./virtual`, so an app with short threads does not load it).
- What a place gives is one element, a `Message` or whatever the thread holds (`Reasoning`, `ToolCall`, a `Note`),
  never none and never two: the room of the messages not drawn is kept as padding, so the scrollbar is the thread's.
- The place of the reader is kept: with a `rowKey`, messages that come in before the ones in sight (older ones loaded, a
  thread read again that now begins earlier) or that replace them do not move what the reader is looking at, while the
  reader is away from the end; at the end the thread stays at the end. It opens at the end, drawing the last messages from
  the first paint. The app reaches the thread through `ref` (`scrollToEnd`, `scrollToStart`, `scrollToIndex`) and the box
  that scrolls through `containerRef`.
- Screen readers meet a log, which announces what is added to it: while the reader is away from the end the log is
  silent (`aria-live="off"`), so the messages that scroll into the page are not read out one after the other.

A long list of which only the rows in sight are in the page: ten thousand messages cost what thirty do. The rows
are the toolkit's own (`ItemRow`, or any `<li>`); this part is the box that scrolls and the choice of which rows to
draw, on TanStack Virtual (`@tanstack/react-virtual`, an npm dependency, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md). It has its own
entry of the package (`./virtual`), so an app with short lists does not load the library.
- The rows of a list are all as tall as each other, so one of them is measured as it is drawn and the rest follow:
  any density holds, and so do the 44px of a finger. `estimateSize` is only where the first paint starts from.
- The room of the rows not drawn is kept as padding, so the scrollbar is the one of the whole list.
- With `variable` the rows are not all as tall (messages of a thread, a few lines or a screenful): each row is
  measured as it is drawn and watched, so a row that grows (an answer being written, an image that arrives) moves
  the ones after it. `estimateSize` is then the height of a row not yet seen, and the scrollbar is as honest as the
  rows seen so far allow.
- A row measured keeps its height where it moves: by its `rowKey` (its id), not its place. The library is given one
  function for the keys and not a new one at every paint (a new one makes it read the key of every row again, ten
  thousand of them, at each paint), and a new one only when the keys changed where the list can see them (its ends and
  the rows drawn).
- For screen readers it is a list that says how many items it holds and where each one is (`aria-setsize`,
  `aria-posinset`): what is not drawn is still counted.
The box needs a height: `fill` makes it as tall as the region that holds it (the content, a pane of `ContentSplit`),
as `Empty fill` and `Page fit` are, so an app writes no class for it; beside other parts in a `Column fill` it takes
what they leave. `pad` is the room inside the box, around the rows, a step of the scale.

A list the user puts in order: each row has a handle that moves it, with the pointer, a finger or the keyboard. The
behaviour is dnd-kit's (`@dnd-kit/core` and `@dnd-kit/sortable`, npm dependencies, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md); the form
is the toolkit's. It has its own entry of the package (`./reorder`), so an app with no such list does not load it.
- The handle is the only thing that drags: the rest of the row keeps its presses, its fields and its text.
  With the keyboard: Space takes the row, the arrows move it, Space puts it down, Escape puts it back. Screen
  readers hear where it is at each step, in the app's words (`words.reorder`). While a row is taken, Escape is
  the list's: a dialog or a sheet the list is in stays open.
- The row taken is raised on the sheet colour with the `float` elevation and no border (R4), and follows the pointer
  up and down only. The others make room for it: at once, or sliding in 200ms where the app has motion on
  (`animated`, or `MotionProvider`), never with reduced motion.
- The list is the app's: `onReorder` gives the new order and the app keeps it. Nothing is kept here.

files.about:
A message of mail being written, with a text that has a little form: who it goes to, its subject, its text, and
the button that sends it. It is on the `./rich-text` entry, with the field its text is written in (TipTap).
The rows are a form read from the top: «To», then «Cc» and «Bcc», which stay behind a button of the «To» row until
they are asked for or hold an address (most messages have neither), the subject, and the text (`RichTextField`:
bold, italic, underline, two lists, a quote; its value is HTML). An address is a chip (`ChipsInput`): a comma, a
semicolon, a blank or Enter closes one, and one that is not an address is said so on its chip, never refused.
The app holds the draft (`value`, `onChange`) and sends it: the composer knows no server. «Send» is the one solid
button (R3); Ctrl+Enter (⌘ Enter) does the same from anywhere in the form, after an address still being typed is
closed into its chip. Enter alone never sends: in the subject it does nothing, in the text it makes a new line.
A message that cannot go (nobody to send it to, an address that is not one) is not sent: the reason is said in
words above the buttons and the focus goes to the row that is wrong.
The names of the rows are at their start, in the muted ink, not above the fields as in a `FormField`: a message
is read down one column of fields, and the names are a margin beside it. While it is being
sent the button waits in its place. «Discard» is there only when the app can throw the draft away, and does it at
once: the app offers Undo in a notice (`Toasts`).

A field for text with a little form: bold, italic and underlined words, two kinds of list, a quote. The editing is
TipTap's (`@tiptap/react` and its starter kit, on ProseMirror: npm dependencies, pinned, see THIRD_PARTY.md); the
form is the toolkit's: the border and the focus ring of a field, and above the text the toolkit's own `Toolbar`
with Sigrid's icons (R6). It has its own entry of the package (`./rich-text`): TipTap is the
heaviest thing the toolkit rests on, and an app that writes no formatted text does not load it.
- What the row of buttons offers is all the field does: headings, code, links and rules are switched off, so a
  paste or a shortcut cannot bring in what the user has no button to take away. The value holds what was written
  and nothing else: no empty paragraph is kept after a list (Enter twice leaves a list or a quote).
- A button that is on (the caret is in bold text) says so with the selection tint, as any switch of a toolbar.
- The value is HTML, the app's to keep: `onChange` gives it at every change. A value that comes from outside (a
  draft opened) replaces the text and is not a step of the undo: Ctrl+Z never brings the other draft back. The
  field's own changes never loop back, also when the app hands them back late (a store, a round trip): a value
  the field itself gave a moment ago is not taken for a new one.
- It takes what a `FormField` gives its control (`id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `required`). A `<label>`
  names only the browser's own fields, so the text finds the label that points at its `id`, takes its name from it
  (`aria-labelledby`) and takes the focus when the label is pressed, as an input does.
- Text is 16px below 860px, so a phone does not zoom, and 14px above.
